newsitem.title: SPAIN: Battle lines harden in Spanish digital TV fight.
newsitem.headline: Battle lines harden in Spanish digital TV fight.

text.p: Spain vowed on Wednesday to press ahead with a reorganisation of its digital television regime, which could scupper the first such project.
And the backers of the first project -- Promotora de Informaciones (Prisa), Canal Plus and Antena 3 -- are standing firm and plan to christen go ahead on schedule on Thursday.

The row, which pits the conservative government against Spain's largest communications group -- the socialist-leaning Prisa -- revolves around tiny decoders that ensure homes receive all channels from all platforms.
The first digital platform, which would be administered by Canalsatellite, has already ordered decoders, but they will not meet the government's new requirement of universality.
In general, digital television, which will be offered as pay television, will be broadcast via satellite to homes, which will require decoders to receive the channels.
The stakes are high in Spain, where there is next to no cable competition, as digital television sales are expected to reach 100 billion pesetas in 2000.

"We can't understand the the government would stop the commercial sale (of the channels). We believe that, if they tried to, that would be unconstitutional," Prisa Managing Director Juan Luis Cebrian told journalists.
Canalsatellite has ordered 10 billion pesetas worth of decoders from Philips Electronics NV and Sony Corp .
"Our decoder is compatible and legal in Europe," Cebrian said. "The government wants to standardise what doesn't exist."
But the Development Ministry said it was essential that the law be changed to protect viewers rights.

"Apart from political valuations, which anyone can make, the facts are that there is a Community norm that requires us to establish technical requirements ensuring the decoders are compatible," Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado told journalists.

The government maintains that the new regime it plans to approve at a cabinet meeting on Friday will protect viewer rights, while Canalsatellite charges the government is abusing its power to favour a second platform.

That platform, backed by Telefonica de Espana, whose remaining state stake of 20.9 percent is being privatised, Radio and Television of Spain (RTVE), Mexican group Televisa and various regional channels and editorial groups. It is not due to launch for several months.
